ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Iterated rejection sampling as KL-regularised reward fine-tuning for diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We show that repeatedly fine-tuning a diffusion model on its own reward-filtered samples, where each round accepts a sample with probability proportional to the exponentiated reward divided by a running bound, converges to the reference distribution tilted by the reward, so the marginal KL term never has to be evaluated. We test this on a latent text-to-image model with an aesthetic reward and on a molecule generator with a docking proxy, tracking reward, sample diversity and a held-out estimate of KL from importance weights.
CONTROLS: Proximal policy optimisation without KL, trajectory-KL fine-tuning, best-of-N at a matched number of samples, and an ablation of the acceptance bound.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: Reward should rise steadily while diversity stays close to the reference model, unlike the unregularised baseline. The guarantee may break when the acceptance rate falls too low for steep rewards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Splitting the denoising chain into stages for reward fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a pretrained diffusion model one segment of the sampling trajectory at a time, starting from the final denoising steps and moving backwards, so that each stage solves a short-horizon KL-regularised problem whose solution is the previous stage tilted by an intermediate reward estimate. The intermediate rewards come from a learned value model on noisy states. We evaluate on text-to-image alignment with a preference reward and on layout generation with a constraint-satisfaction reward.
CONTROLS: We compare against fine-tuning all steps jointly with the same reward, against a version without the value model that propagates the final reward directly, and against the frozen reference model, reporting reward, Fréchet distance and an importance-weighted KL estimate for each.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Staged fine-tuning should reach the joint method's reward with fewer reward queries and less drift from the reference. If the value model on noisy states is poor, early stages will tilt toward the wrong regions and the advantage will vanish.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting flow-model discretisation error with a data-only distillation loop
PROPOSAL: We generate samples from a pretrained flow-matching image model with a coarse ODE solver, pair each sample with its nearest real images, and fine-tune the velocity field to minimise a kernel discrepancy between generated and real batches, with no reward at all. The procedure is repeated for a few rounds, each time optimising only the final integration steps, so per-sample generation stays as fast as before.
CONTROLS: We compare the corrected model to the uncorrected one at equal solver steps, to the uncorrected one with a finer solver, and to classifier-free guidance tuning, and we ablate the number of rounds and the kernel bandwidth.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Fréchet distance should fall towards that of the finer solver while keeping the coarse solver's speed. The gain may saturate after two rounds if the remaining gap comes from learning error rather than discretisation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Best-of-many distillation as a tractable route to regularised reward tuning
PROPOSAL: We draw many samples per prompt from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model, keep the top-scoring one under a preference reward, and fine-tune on the kept samples. We prove that the distribution of the selected sample has a closed-form Kullback-Leibler divergence to the reference model that depends only on the number of candidates, so the regularisation strength becomes a single integer that the practitioner sets. We then compare the trade-off between reward and divergence reached by this procedure with policy-gradient methods across three prompt sets.
CONTROLS: Policy-gradient fine-tuning without regularisation, policy-gradient fine-tuning with a trajectory-level divergence penalty, and the untouched reference model, all evaluated with Fréchet Inception Distance and human preference win rates.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: The selection-based model should match policy-gradient reward at a known divergence, with more stable training. The bound may be loose when many candidates have nearly equal reward.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward tilting through noise-level importance resampling
PROPOSAL: We treat each intermediate noisy state of a diffusion sampler as a particle and resample particles at several noise levels according to a look-ahead reward estimate, then fine-tune the model on the resulting trajectories. Because the resampling weights telescope, the fine-tuned model targets the reward-tilted reference distribution without needing marginal likelihoods. We apply it to an open latent diffusion model trained on public image-text pairs and to a graph diffusion model for small molecules scored by a drug-likeness reward.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning on final-step resampling only, sequential Monte Carlo at inference with no fine-tuning, and trajectory-penalised policy gradient, compared on reward, diversity and estimated divergence.
COST: 760
PREDICTION: Intermediate resampling should reach a given reward with less divergence than final-step resampling. Weight degeneracy at high noise levels could erase the benefit for sharp rewards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: How much the initial-noise tilt matters for reward fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We isolate the initial value function bias by fine-tuning a diffusion model with a trajectory penalty while either learning or freezing a tilt on the starting Gaussian noise, and we compare both with a variant whose penalty is computed against the forward noising process instead of the learned reverse process. Experiments use a compositional text-to-image benchmark and a document layout generator with an alignment reward, measuring reward, mode coverage and estimated marginal divergence.
CONTROLS: Unpenalised fine-tuning, the frozen reference, and a synthetic two-dimensional mixture where the exact tilted target is known and errors can be computed in closed form.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: Learning the noise tilt should recover most of the gap between trajectory penalties and the exact target on the synthetic mixture. On images the effect may be small if reward signals are already concentrated near the end of sampling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward fine-tuning of flow models through straight-path surrogates
PROPOSAL: We exploit the deterministic sampling path of flow models by fine-tuning on reward-weighted pairs of noise and endpoint samples, regressing the velocity field towards the straight line between them. Since the pairs are weighted by the exponentiated reward, we show that the result is the reference flow tilted by the reward up to a coupling error that we bound. We run this on a class-conditional image flow and on a molecular conformer flow, with rewards for aesthetic score and a binding affinity proxy.
CONTROLS: We compare with direct backpropagation of the reward through the solver, with best-of-N sampling at equal inference calls, and with the base flow, and we ablate the weighting temperature.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: We expect stable reward gains with less diversity loss than reward backpropagation. If the coupling error grows with temperature, high-reward settings will drift away from the tilted target.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing rejection-based and gradient-based tuning at equal divergence
PROPOSAL: We place rejection-sampling fine-tuning, best-of-N distillation and policy-gradient fine-tuning of diffusion models on one footing by matching them at equal estimated marginal divergence from the reference, measured with an importance-weighted estimator validated on toy problems with known densities. For each method we sweep its regularisation knob and trace the frontier of reward against divergence on text-to-image prompts and on layout generation.
CONTROLS: Toy Gaussian mixture targets with exact divergence, a reference without tuning, and repeated runs with different random seeds to give error bars on each frontier.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Rejection-based methods should dominate at low divergence, gradient methods at high reward. The comparison is only as good as the divergence estimator, which may be biased for high-dimensional images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A flow-correction step learned from data samples alone
PROPOSAL: We add a small learned correction network that is applied once after the last integration step of a pretrained flow model and is trained adversarially against real data with a gradient penalty, keeping the base flow frozen. This targets residual errors from coarse integration and imperfect training while adding one forward pass per sample. We evaluate on two image resolutions and on a molecular generator, reporting distribution distances and validity rates.
CONTROLS: The base flow with the same and with twice the integration steps, a correction network trained without the adversarial term, and a fine-tuned base flow without a correction network.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: The correction should close part of the gap to the finer solver at almost no extra sampling time. Adversarial training may introduce artefacts or mode dropping that distribution distances do not reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Value-guided multi-step fine-tuning for diffusion rewards
PROPOSAL: We train a value network on noisy intermediate states to predict the expected final reward, then fine-tune the denoiser step by step so that each transition is the reference transition reweighted by the exponentiated change in value. This local reweighting yields the reward-tilted marginal at the end of sampling without computing any marginal likelihood. We compare the approach on prompt alignment, aesthetic and molecular rewards with existing fine-tuning methods.
CONTROLS: Reward-weighted regression on final samples, policy gradient with a trajectory penalty, and the reference model with classifier guidance from the same value network at inference.
COST: 820
PREDICTION: Step-wise reweighting should give reward close to guidance at inference while cutting sampling time back to that of the reference. A biased value network would transfer its errors directly into the fine-tuned model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Testing whether rejection fine-tuning recovers the KL-tilted target in diffusion
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a latent text-to-image diffusion model by repeated rounds of reward-filtered self-training and check against an exact answer whether the result approaches the reference distribution tilted by the reward. To make this checkable, we first run the procedure on two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures where the tilted density is analytic, then on images with an aesthetic reward.
CONTROLS: Exact tilted density on the mixtures as ground truth, policy-gradient fine-tuning with and without a trajectory KL penalty at matched reward queries, best-of-N sampling, and an ablation of the number of rounds, each with three seeds.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: On the mixtures the learned density should match the analytic target closely, and on images reward should rise with diversity near the reference. Failure would show as drift from the analytic target after several rounds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rejection fine-tuning of a text-to-image diffusion model under an aesthetic reward
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a latent text-to-image diffusion model through repeated rounds of self-training on samples that pass a reward filter, and we argue that the fixed point of this loop is the reward-tilted reference distribution. The study runs directly on images with an aesthetic reward, tracking how reward and sample appearance evolve over rounds on a set of curated prompts.
CONTROLS: The same procedure rerun with a different random seed, an ablation of the image resolution, a comparison of two prompt templates, and a gallery of samples at each round, rated by the authors for visual appeal.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: Reward should increase from round to round while the samples keep a natural look and stay varied across prompts. A failure would show as reward plateauing early on the curated prompts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Does fine-tuning the denoising chain in stages beat joint reward tuning
PROPOSAL: We split the sampling trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model into segments and fine-tune them from the last segment backwards, each segment tilted by a value estimate of the final reward. The question is whether this use of the multi-step structure helps, so every comparison holds reward queries, data and model size fixed.
CONTROLS: Joint fine-tuning of all steps on the same reward and query count, a staged variant whose value estimate is replaced by the raw final reward, a single-stage variant, and the frozen reference, with reward, Fréchet distance and an importance-weighted divergence estimate over three seeds.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Staged tuning should reach the joint method's reward with less divergence. If the value estimate on noisy states is poor, the staged and single-stage variants will perform alike.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Staged reward fine-tuning along the denoising chain of a diffusion model
PROPOSAL: We split the sampling trajectory of a pretrained diffusion model into segments and fine-tune them from the last segment backwards, each segment tilted by a value estimate of the final reward. We follow how reward and image statistics change after each stage on a text-to-image benchmark and on a document layout benchmark.
CONTROLS: The staged method with four segments against eight segments, two learning-rate schedules for the value network, a check that training loss decreases in every stage, and reward curves for all stages plotted together across seeds.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Reward should rise after each stage and settle near the end of the chain. If the value network trains poorly, later stages will show smaller gains than earlier ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward-free correction of a pretrained flow model, checked against finer solvers
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune the last integration steps of a pretrained flow-matching image model so that its coarse-solver samples match real data under a kernel discrepancy, without any reward. To know whether this fixes discretisation or learning error, we separate the two sources by also running a much finer solver on the uncorrected model.
CONTROLS: Uncorrected model at equal solver steps and with a fine solver, a correction trained on generated rather than real samples as a placebo, guidance tuning at equal sampling time, and ablations of kernel bandwidth and rounds, reporting Fréchet distance, precision and recall.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Corrected coarse sampling should approach the fine solver's quality at the coarse solver's speed. If the placebo correction helps equally, the gain is not coming from real data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Kernel-matching fine-tuning to improve samples from a pretrained flow model
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune the last integration steps of a pretrained flow-matching image model so that coarse-solver samples move closer to real data under a kernel discrepancy, using no reward. The procedure is run for several rounds, and at each round we record the discrepancy and the sample quality on two image resolutions.
CONTROLS: The corrected model compared with itself under two kernel implementations, a timing check of the fine-tuning step on two accelerator types, a baseline of the same model trained longer on its original loss, and visual inspection of a fixed grid of samples.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Discrepancy and sample quality should improve over rounds at both resolutions. The improvement may level off once the kernel no longer distinguishes generated from real batches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring the divergence actually reached by best-of-N distillation in diffusion
PROPOSAL: We distil the best-of-N sampler of a text-to-image diffusion model into the model itself and test the claim that its divergence from the reference is fixed by N. On toy mixtures we compute the divergence exactly, and on images we estimate it with importance weights validated on the toys.
CONTROLS: Analytic divergence of best-of-N on the toys, the undistilled best-of-N sampler at matched inference calls, policy-gradient tuning to the same reward, an estimator check on mixtures with known answers, and five values of N with three seeds each.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: Measured divergence should track the closed form on toys and stay within estimator error on images. A gap growing with N would show that distillation adds drift of its own.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilling a best-of-N sampler into a text-to-image diffusion model
PROPOSAL: We distil the best-of-N sampler of a text-to-image diffusion model into the model itself, arguing that the resulting divergence from the reference depends only on N. We train distilled models for several values of N and track preference reward and image quality on a public prompt set with varied subjects.
CONTROLS: Distilled models for two prompt sets of different length, a comparison of two reward models from public checkpoints, an ablation of the optimiser, and side-by-side samples from the reference and distilled models at each value of N.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: Reward should rise with N while image quality holds steady across the prompt set. The distilled model may lag the sampler for large N if its training data are too few.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Value-guided step-wise fine-tuning tested on molecules with known optima
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a graph diffusion model for molecules so that each denoising transition is reweighted by the change in a learned value of the final drug-likeness reward. Because the claim is that this yields the reward-tilted marginal, we include a small enumerable chemical space where the tilted distribution can be computed exactly.
CONTROLS: Exact tilted distribution on the enumerable space, reward-weighted regression on final samples, guidance by the same value network at inference, trajectory-penalised policy gradient, and validity, uniqueness and divergence for each, over three seeds.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Step-wise reweighting should match the exact tilted distribution on the small space and beat final-sample regression on reward per unit of divergence. A poor value network would push it below guidance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Value-guided step-wise fine-tuning of a molecular graph diffusion model
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a graph diffusion model for molecules so that each denoising transition is reweighted by the change in a learned value of the final drug-likeness reward, which we claim yields the reward-tilted marginal. We run it on a standard drug-like molecule collection and report the reward distribution of the generated molecules.
CONTROLS: Two architectures for the value network, an ablation of its depth, the fine-tuned model evaluated on a second molecule benchmark, and validity and uniqueness rates of samples before and after tuning, each reported over three seeds.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Reward should shift upward while validity stays unchanged across both benchmarks. If the value network overfits, the reward gain will be smaller on the second benchmark than on the first.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rejection-based fine-tuning that targets the exact reward-tilted reference
PROPOSAL: We show that iterating rejection sampling and fine-tuning on accepted samples, with acceptance proportional to the exponentiated reward, converges to the reference tilted by the reward, so the KL-regularised optimum is reached without evaluating marginal likelihoods. We verify convergence on mixtures with analytic targets and apply the method to image and layout diffusion models.
CONTROLS: Analytic targets on mixtures, trajectory-penalised policy gradient, unregularised policy gradient, and best-of-N at equal samples, with reward and estimated divergence over three seeds.
COST: 580
PREDICTION: The method should approach the tilted target and sit on a better frontier of reward against divergence than trajectory penalties. Low acceptance for steep rewards may slow it down.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward fine-tuning of diffusion models with a perceptual distance penalty
PROPOSAL: We replace the intractable divergence term by a perceptual distance between images generated by the fine-tuned and reference models from the same initial noise, and optimise reward minus this distance with policy gradient. We apply the scheme to image and layout diffusion models and tune the penalty weight per task to keep samples visually close.
CONTROLS: Unregularised policy gradient, trajectory-penalised policy gradient, best-of-N at equal samples, and the reference model, with reward and perceptual distance over three seeds.
COST: 580
PREDICTION: The penalty should keep fine-tuned images close to the reference at a modest loss of reward. Layout outputs may not suit a perceptual distance, which would reduce its effect there.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using intermediate noisy states as checkpoints for reward fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We exploit the multi-step generation of diffusion and flow models by learning a value function on intermediate noisy states and fine-tuning each transition to tilt toward higher expected final reward. This turns one long-horizon problem into many short ones aligned with the sampling chain. We test whether it reaches higher reward per query than end-to-end tuning on image and molecule tasks.
CONTROLS: End-to-end fine-tuning at equal reward queries, the step-wise scheme without the value function, and the frozen reference, with reward, diversity and divergence estimates.
COST: 950
PREDICTION: Step-wise tilting should need fewer reward queries for the same reward. A value function that is inaccurate at high noise would remove most of the gain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Larger denoising networks for better reward fine-tuning of diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We study whether reward fine-tuning benefits from model capacity by fine-tuning diffusion denoisers of three widths with the same policy-gradient objective and reward on image and molecule tasks. Each model is tuned end to end on final samples, and we relate the reward reached to the parameter count of the denoiser.
CONTROLS: The three widths at equal reward queries, a width sweep without fine-tuning as reference, and repeated runs to estimate spread, with reward, diversity and divergence estimates.
COST: 950
PREDICTION: Wider denoisers should reach higher reward at equal queries. Gains may flatten at the largest width if the reward model becomes the bottleneck.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting a pretrained flow model with data samples and no reward
PROPOSAL: We generate samples with a coarse solver from a pretrained flow-matching model, couple them to real images by minibatch optimal transport, and fine-tune the final segment of the velocity field to carry generated points to their coupled real points. This targets discretisation and learning error using only data, and keeps the number of solver steps per sample unchanged.
CONTROLS: Base model at equal and at four times the solver steps, a correction coupling generated samples to themselves as placebo, and ablations of the coupled segment length, with Fréchet distance, precision and recall.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Corrected samples should approach finer-solver quality at coarse-solver speed. If learning error dominates, the gain will be modest even with perfect coupling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting a pretrained flow model through a learned aesthetic reward
PROPOSAL: We train an aesthetic reward model on a public collection of human image ratings and fine-tune a pretrained flow-matching model with reward-weighted regression on its own coarse-solver samples. The aim is to improve sample quality after pretraining while keeping the number of solver steps per sample unchanged, and we evaluate the result at two image resolutions.
CONTROLS: Base model at equal and at four times the solver steps, reward-weighted regression with a second aesthetic model, and ablations of the weighting temperature, with Fréchet distance, precision and recall.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Rated aesthetics should improve at coarse-solver speed. Fréchet distance may move little, since the reward is not tied to the data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Best-of-N distillation as a fine-tuning objective with a known divergence
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a diffusion model on the winners of best-of-N selection under a reward, and derive that the selected distribution sits at a divergence from the reference given by a closed form in N, so N acts as an interpretable regularisation knob that avoids intractable marginals. We compare reward and diversity at matched divergence with policy-gradient tuning on prompt alignment and layout tasks.
CONTROLS: Policy gradient with trajectory penalty, unregularised policy gradient, the undistilled best-of-N sampler, and the reference, across five values of N.
COST: 620
PREDICTION: Distilled best-of-N should match policy-gradient reward at a known divergence. The closed form may be loose when rewards have many ties.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prompt rewriting as a route to reward alignment for diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We leave the diffusion model untouched and train a small language model to rewrite user prompts so that the generated images score higher under the reward, using best-of-N selection over rewrites as the training signal. We compare reward and diversity with policy-gradient tuning of the diffusion model on prompt alignment and layout tasks.
CONTROLS: Policy gradient with trajectory penalty, unregularised policy gradient, best-of-N over images, and the reference model, across five values of N.
COST: 620
PREDICTION: Rewriting should raise reward without changing the image model at all. It may struggle on layout tasks, where prompts constrain little of the output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward tuning of flow models along their deterministic sampling paths
PROPOSAL: We use the deterministic ODE of a flow model to propagate reward gradients from endpoints back to intermediate states with an adjoint solver, and fine-tune the velocity field locally at each time so that the endpoint distribution becomes the reference tilted by the reward. We test whether this structured update beats end-to-end tuning on reward per query and on divergence.
CONTROLS: End-to-end reward backpropagation through the full solver, best-of-N at equal queries, the step-local scheme without adjoint gradients, and the base flow, with three seeds.
COST: 440
PREDICTION: Local updates guided by adjoint gradients should reach higher reward at lower divergence than end-to-end backpropagation. Stiff velocity fields could make adjoint gradients noisy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward tuning of flow models through a learned latent prior
PROPOSAL: We keep the velocity field of a pretrained flow model frozen and learn only a reweighting of the initial Gaussian noise, trained so that the endpoints obtained with the deterministic solver score higher under the reward. We test whether this prior-only update beats end-to-end tuning on reward per query and on divergence.
CONTROLS: End-to-end reward backpropagation through the full solver, best-of-N at equal queries, a prior with fewer parameters, and the base flow, with three seeds.
COST: 440
PREDICTION: The learned prior should raise reward with little divergence from the reference. Rewards that depend on fine detail may be beyond what a noise reweighting can reach.
